question: What is the primary cause of inherited degenerative disorders?

options.B: Exposure to environmental toxins at work
options.C: Faulty genes passed down through families
options.D: Nutritional deficiencies in the daily diet

explanation: These conditions stem directly from genetic mutations inherited from biological parents rather than environmental or infectious agents. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h1)

question: Why is the management of inherited degenerative disorders primarily focused on prevention and support?

options.A: Patients usually refuse all forms of medical treatment
options.B: Hospital resources are insufficient for long-term care
options.C: Genetic disorders always resolve spontaneously with age
options.D: The underlying genetic mutations cannot be cured once present

explanation: Because the root cause lies within the permanent DNA structure, modern medicine focuses on slowing progression, managing symptoms, and preventing transmission. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h1)

question: How many generations should a nurse typically map when taking a detailed family genetic history?
explanation: Mapping three generations allows clinicians to trace inheritance patterns, skipped generations, and familial traits accurately. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h2)

question: A nurse constructs a family pedigree primarily to achieve what clinical goal?

options.A: Diagnose infectious diseases spread within the local community
options.B: Evaluate the nutritional status of elderly household members
options.C: Determine the exact financial cost of long-term patient care
options.D: Identify hereditary disease patterns and individuals at genetic risk

explanation: Pedigrees visually display health conditions across family lines to highlight who might inherit or carry a genetic disorder. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h2)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention regarding inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: To stop genetic diseases before conception occurs
options.B: To cure symptoms after the disease has fully developed
options.C: To provide physical therapy for disabled children
options.D: To lower the cost of hospital medications

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping the occurrence of a condition altogether through education, lifestyle choices, and pre-conception counseling. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h3)

question: A nurse in a local Nigerian clinic educates young couples about the importance of knowing their genotype before marriage. Which level of prevention does this represent?
explanation: Pre-marital genotype screening and counseling aim to prevent affected conceptions entirely, which defines primary prevention. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h3)

question: What defines an individual who is a 'carrier' of an autosomal recessive genetic disorder?

options.A: They have two mutant gene copies causing rapid degeneration
options.B: They display severe physical symptoms of the actual disease
options.C: They are completely immune to all forms of genetic illness
options.D: They possess one mutant gene copy and show no symptoms

explanation: Carriers have a single altered gene alongside a normal gene, protecting them from the disease while allowing potential transmission. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: Why is pre-test and post-test counseling essential when conducting carrier screening tests?

options.A: To prepare clients for the emotional and social impact of results
options.B: To force the patient to pay for expensive hospital equipment
options.C: To diagnose unrelated infectious diseases during the session
options.D: To ensure the laboratory technician processes the blood faster

explanation: Genetic findings carry heavy emotional weight and potential stigma, requiring professional support before and after testing. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h4)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of secondary prevention in a newborn?

options.A: Routine newborn screening for congenital metabolic disorders
options.B: Conducting community town halls on environmental health
options.C: Administering long-term physical therapy for adult paralysis
options.D: Providing genetic counseling to prospective parents before marriage

explanation: Newborn screening detects hidden anomalies early in life so treatment can start before severe symptoms manifest. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of early detection through secondary prevention screening?

options.A: It guarantees a complete cure for all degenerative illnesses
options.B: It removes the need for any future medical appointments
options.C: Prompt intervention can slow disease progression and minimize damage
options.D: It completely eliminates the mutated genes from the human body

explanation: While it cannot cure the genetic defect, early detection allows medical teams to intervene before permanent tissue destruction occurs. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h5)

question: A parent expresses intense guilt after learning they passed a genetic disorder to their child. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Provide a supportive, non-judgmental space to validate their complex emotions
options.B: Explain that genetic inheritance is a deliberate choice they made
options.C: Tell the parent firmly that dwelling on the past is a waste of time
options.D: Ignore the emotional comment and focus entirely on charting vital signs

explanation: Parents often struggle with self-blame, requiring compassionate nursing presence and emotional validation without judgment. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: What is a core component of nursing advocacy in genetic healthcare?

options.A: Protecting patient autonomy and defending their right to healthcare
options.B: Reporting carriers of genetic diseases to public newspapers
options.C: Deciding which medical treatment the family must accept
options.D: Charging patients fees for counseling services provided

explanation: Advocacy ensures patients retain their decision-making power and receive fair, unbiased care free from coercion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h6)

question: What is the main role of the nurse within a multidisciplinary degenerative care team?

options.A: Replacing the dietician and physiotherapist during hospital shifts
options.B: Performing all specialized surgical procedures independently
options.C: Making final legal decisions regarding patient insurance coverage
options.D: Acting as a central communication hub between the family and specialists

explanation: Nurses coordinate care across different disciplines to ensure smooth communication and holistic patient management. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team necessary for patients with inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Specialists alone can handle all emotional and social family needs
options.B: Hospital policies mandate that at least five doctors see every patient
options.C: The conditions affect multiple body systems and require diverse expertise
options.D: Nurses are not qualified to provide any form of direct care

explanation: Because degenerative disorders cause widespread physical and metabolic decline, input from various specialists ensures comprehensive support. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T20#GNS222_U4_T20_h7)
